source_read: PDF, pp. 242–248 (all 7 pages read; Figures 1–3 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi; Figure 2 also read from a 300-dpi crop)

claims.note: This paper has no DAT data. It bears on the claim as context for the same five people: it describes the programme (drug court, daily centre visits, cognitive behaviour therapy, jail on relapse, random urine tests) and states that the few who stayed abstinent may not be representative. The authors also re-read the DAT increase as adaptation in surviving terminals rather than reversal of damage. Nothing here contradicts the claim. The claim's 'treatment programme' could specify 'drug-court-supervised rehabilitation programme'.

anchors.extracted: The 5 retested users (3 women, 2 men; 29 ± 3 years; scanned at 3 ± 1.6 and 14 ± 2 months of abstinence) are the 5 of the original 12 who stayed drug-free for 9 months, the same five as the DAT follow-up. Programme: California drug-court monitoring rehabilitation, weekly or biweekly drug screens plus daily centre visits.

Few stayed abstinent and may not be representative; relapsers were excluded from follow-up; urine tests were random within 2-week periods, so intermittent use could be missed; participants attended daily, received cognitive behaviour therapy and faced jail if they relapsed.

anchors.locator: Discussion › 'Recovery of Thalamic but Not Striatal Metabolism…', 1st paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Because striatal metabolism stayed low, the authors suggest the earlier DAT increases reflect adaptation in surviving terminals rather than reversal of damage.

claims.overstatement: Slight. (1) 'Striatal metabolism did not change' should read 'did not change significantly': +2.7% (SD 6.7%) in 5 people (my paired t≈0.9) cannot show no change. (2) The thalamic rise is in relative (region/global) values only: absolute thalamic metabolism did not change significantly, and global metabolism fell from 42.6 to 40.8 µmol/100 g/min (about −4%, not significant). Part of the relative rise may therefore come from the denominator. Suggest stating both.
claims.note: All numbers checked against p. 244 and Figure 1: thalamus +12% (SD 9%), striatum +2.7%, occipital +0.4%, n=5; thalamus 1.11 vs 1.31 (short) and 1.23 vs 1.31 (protracted). Errors in test statistics confirmed and extended. (a) A paired test in 5 people has df=4, not 9. (b) 12% (SD 9%) with n=5 gives t≈2.98 (p≈0.04), not the printed 2.3. (c) The striatal t=1.3 (df=9) matches 10 observations, not 5 people; with n=5 I get t≈0.9. (d) The occipital t=1.2 cannot arise from a mean of 0.4% with SD 9% (t≈0.1). My recomputation for protracted thalamus vs controls (n=13 vs 11): t≈−2.1, p≈0.05, d≈−0.84 (95% CI −1.68 to −0.01). 'Not different' is therefore borderline and leaves a large difference possible. The claim's 'reported as not different' wording is appropriate. Group sizes are inconsistent within the paper: the protracted group is 10 in Methods but 13 by df and in later text, and the short group is 7 in the Introduction/Subjects but 12 in the analyses.

anchors.extracted: 5 users scanned after short (<6 months; mean 3, SD 1.6) and protracted (12–17 months; mean 14, SD 2) abstinence; 8 more scanned once at 17 ± 10 months; 11 controls (7 women, 4 men; 31 ± 7 years) scanned once.

anchors.locator: Results › 'Brain Metabolism in Methamphetamine Users After Short and Protracted Abstinence Intervals', 1st paragraph; Figure 1
anchors.extracted: Global 42.6 (SD 4.0) vs 40.8 (SD 3.4), no difference; no difference in absolute striatal, thalamic or occipital metabolism. Relative thalamus +12% (SD 9%), t=2.3, df=9, p<0.05; striatum +2.7% (SD 6.7%), t=1.3, df=9, p<0.23; occipital +0.4% (SD 9%), t=1.2, df=9, p<0.28. Figure 1: all 5 thalamic values rose (roughly +3% to +27%); striatal values mixed, one fell.

anchors.locator: Results › 'Comparison of Healthy Subjects With Methamphetamine Users…', 1st–2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Relative values, controls: caudate 1.35 (0.06), putamen 1.41 (0.09), thalamus 1.31 (0.10). Short abstinence (df=21, i.e. n=12): caudate 1.2 (0.1), t=−4.4; putamen 1.31 (0.08), t=−2.8; thalamus 1.11 (0.08), t=−5.3, p<0.0001. Protracted (df=22, i.e. n=13): caudate 1.23 (0.09), t=−4.4; putamen 1.29 (0.1), t=−3.1, p<0.006; thalamus 1.23 (0.09), described as not different. Absolute global: short 38.5, protracted 37.3, controls 33.8, not significantly different.

anchors.locator: Results › 'Comparison Between Methamphetamine Users Tested After Short Versus Protracted…'
anchors.extracted: Relative thalamus lower in the 12 short- than the 13 protracted-abstinence users (t=−3.8, df=23, p<0.001); striatum not different. The 5 retested people are in both groups.

Methods state 10 protracted-abstinence users (5 retested + 5 of the 8 tested once) and paired t tests; reported df (22, 23) imply 13; the paired-change df=9 is impossible for 5 people. Controls were scanned once only, so test–retest change in non-users is unknown.
Authors note that higher whole-brain metabolism in users, if real, could contribute to the lower relative striatal values.

key_findings.correction: Note recomputed: t=2.3 with df=4 gives p≈0.08; 12% (SD 9%), n=5 gives t≈2.98, p≈0.04. 'Did not change' for striatum/occipital is better as 'no significant change'. The striatal t (1.3) fits n=10, not 5, and the occipital t (1.2) cannot arise from 0.4% (SD 9%).
Editors' calculation reproduced: d≈−0.84; p≈0.051 with n=13 and ≈0.070 with n=10.
Values match the footnotes of Figure 2 (p. 245). The Timed Gait relation is plotted with a negative slope while r is printed unsigned. See 'missed' for a sign problem in this figure.

reporting_issues.note: Extend to the other two regions (striatum t=1.3 fits 10 observations; occipital t=1.2 is impossible from the printed mean and SD).

Also the short-abstinence group: the Introduction and Subjects describe it as the 7 non-completers (p. 243), while the analyses use the original 12 (df=21), which include the 5 retested. The short-vs-protracted unpaired test (12 vs 13, df=23, p. 245) therefore counts the same 5 people in both groups.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. Add: the thalamic 'recovery' is in relative values only; absolute thalamic metabolism did not change significantly and global metabolism fell about 4% (p. 244).

missed: Reporting issue (Figure 2, p. 245, vs Volkow 2001b, p. 9416): the score changes in Figure 2 cannot be reconciled with the means reported for the same five people. Volkow 2001b gives Timed Gait 10.0 to 8.6 s (faster) and delayed recall 11.6 to 12.8 words (more). In Figure 2 the mean '% change in score' is about +13% for Timed Gait and about −12% for delayed recall (also about −13% for Symbol Digit), and the sign convention is not stated. Read as later-minus-earlier, the figure shows most of the five getting slower and recalling fewer words, which contradicts 2001b. Read as earlier-minus-later (the convention consistent with 2001b), all three 'significant' correlations run the other way: larger thalamic increases went with smaller improvements. The abstract's 'associated with improved performance' rests on this figure.

The thalamic increase is in relative values only: absolute thalamic metabolism did not change significantly and global metabolism fell from 42.6 to 40.8 µmol/100 g/min (p. 244). The authors themselves note that normalization can shape relative values (p. 247).

Cross-sectional global metabolism: users (short 38.5, protracted 37.3) were not significantly higher than these 11 controls (33.8) (p. 244). The 12 short-abstinence users are the same people who, in Volkow 2001c, were part of a group 14% above a 21-person control group (p<0.05). This bears on cl_meth_glucose_metabolism: against a different set of 11 controls, a difference of similar size (38.5 vs 33.8, about 14%) was not significant (my d≈0.6, 95% CI −0.25 to 1.42). The users are not an independent sample.

The stated rationale that the tests were those previously correlated with DAT (pp. 243, 247) does not fit the Symbol Digit Modalities Test, which did not correlate with DAT in Volkow 2001a (only Trail Making approached significance among exploratory tests) and was not among the tests reported in the 2001b follow-up.
The SPM figure shows only short abstinence vs controls (Figure 3, p. 246); the protracted-abstinence SPM results (nucleus accumbens decreases) are described but not shown.
Minor: r=0.96 with df=3 gives p≈0.0095, printed as p<0.009 (Figure 2 footnote c).
